lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah make the case for gig work
lead.head: In praise of the odd job

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 124

body: Amit Varma opened with a tall tale. Sipping a bour­bon, he said, he built a gig app called Bourbon Company to find a new co-host every week. Every week, only Ajay Shah ap­plied. {124-J01}
“What should have been a one-night stand be­came an af­fair,” Varma said. The gig econ­omy, he con­cluded, is a strange and cu­ri­ous thing.
Then the hosts got down to busi­ness: the critics’ case against gig work, their an­swers to it, and why, as the episode’s title has it, gig work is awe­some.

Gig work, Shah ex­plained, is a two-sided mar­ket in which buy­ers and sell­ers of labour agree on small tasks with­out com­pli­cated con­tracts. An em­ployer puts a job into an elec­tronic sys­tem; a worker goes into the sys­tem and takes it.

It comes in three kinds, he said: cap­i­tal-intensive gigs, like driv­ing your own car for Uber; skill-intensive ones, like a hair­dresser who comes to your home; and mi­cro­tasks, like la­belling a pho­to­graph.
## The man­ager is sacked
In one sense, Shah said, none of this is new. Indian towns have had their naka or chowk, a spot mar­ket for a day’s labour, for cen­turies.

In an­other sense it is huge. GPS, rat­ings and dig­i­tal ex­haust let an al­go­rithm do a manager’s job, so the man­ager goes and the em­ployee be­comes an out­side con­trac­tor. That, he said, is a mile­stone in the econ­o­mist Ronald Coase’s the­ory of the firm. {124-C02}
“The per­son who in­vented gig work should get a Bharat Ratna,” Shah de­clared. Varma ob­jected that it came out of spon­ta­neous order: “It was not one cen­tral plan­ner who in­vented it.”
## For the de­fence

At Varma’s re­quest, Shah then steel­manned the op­po­si­tion: lost en­ti­tle­ments, volatile in­come, no ca­reer lad­der, bosses that are al­go­rithms and watch too closely, iso­lated work­ers, and Indians paid low piece rates to train the AI that will re­place them.
His first an­swer to all of it was free­dom and con­sent. “Nobody forces ei­ther the buyer or the seller to par­tic­i­pate in gig work,” he said. {124-C03}
An al­go­rith­mic boss, he ar­gued, is more pre­dictable than a tyran­ni­cal human one, and closer mon­i­tor­ing should push a worker’s pay up, not down.

Varma re­cast the ar­gu­ment in terms of out­comes. However de­mean­ing gig work looks from an air-conditioned mid­dle-class room, he said, peo­ple choose it be­cause their other op­tions, from un­em­ploy­ment to beg­ging, are worse.
## A list of ten
Then Varma of­fered ten rea­sons why gig work is awe­some. “Five of them are eco­nomic rea­sons, three are so­cial, two are eth­i­cal and they kind of bleed into one an­other,” he said. {124-C09}
They ran from an easy way into the city and work that sur­vived COVID to open­ness across caste and re­li­gion and the dig­nity of work.
In India, Shah said, the case is stronger still. Only about 440 mil­lion peo­ple work in a coun­try of 1.4 to 1.5 bil­lion, and only about 10 per cent have pro­tected for­mal jobs.
Gig work, he and Maitreesh Ghatak had ar­gued in an ar­ti­cle, is an urban safety net: an NREGS for the cities that no gov­ern­ment had to build. {124-C13}
It shares two of the three virtues Professor Kirit Parikh saw in the NREGS, Shah said: it is self-targeting and self-adjusting.
“Public goods through vol­un­tary pri­vate ac­tion,” Varma said. Then he had one last ques­tion: “And you co-wrote that ar­ti­cle with a Bengali econ­o­mist, didn’t you?”

second.label: Microtasks
second.head: Piecework goes global
second.deck: Ajay Shah on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and India’s share of the world’s microtasks

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Amazon Mechanical Turk

body: Amazon in­vented the mi­cro­task busi­ness, Ajay Shah said, with Amazon Mechanical Turk. A worker reads a task de­scrip­tion, takes a short train­ing course, passes a small exam and then does the task again and again, for a piece rate of a rupee or ten ru­pees. {124-S03}
On the other side, a firm de­scribes a task it wants done by a hun­dred or a mil­lion peo­ple, sets the exam and up­loads the data. Amazon farms the work out and re­turns the an­swers.
Shah seemed to re­call read­ing that Indian work­ers ac­count for 40 per cent of the mi­cro­tasks done in the whole world. {#forty} “This is just some­thing great that has hap­pened,” he said.

quote.text: And this is noth­ing short of a mir­a­cle.

third.head: Don’t tip the sand seller

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the price of sand

body: Critics say gig work­ers who label pho­to­graphs are the foun­da­tion on which AI gi­ants built tril­lions of dol­lars of mar­ket value. {#trillions} Since the work­ers are paid low piece rates in India, that looks un­fair.

By that logic, Ajay Shah replied, the whole Indian ser­vices rev­o­lu­tion was un­fair. American Express and JP Morgan ran call cen­tres in India; no­body should say JP Morgan’s mar­ket value was built on the backs of un­der­paid staff in Gurgaon. {124-C08}
His anal­ogy was sand. A com­pany mak­ing ultra-pure poly­crys­talline sil­i­con for in­te­grated cir­cuits buys sand. Its ex­pen­sive out­put is no rea­son to pay the sand seller more.
“The price of sand should be shaped by sup­ply and de­mand, by the price sys­tem,” Shah said. A wage and a mar­ket value, he ar­gued, are not a mean­ing­ful com­par­i­son.

box.title: The paper behind the firm
box.text: In *The Nature of the Firm*[[x1]], Ronald Coase asked what a firm[[x2]] does in­side its bound­ary, with man­agers and long-term em­ploy­ees, and what it buys through arm’s-length con­tracts. Gig work, Ajay Shah said, re­opens that ques­tion, a mile­stone in the his­tory of the firm. {124-C02}

sections.label: Defining the gig
sections.head: The firm redraws its border
sections.caption: the boundary of the firm
body: Gig work, Ajay Shah said, sounds fancier than it is. An em­ployer who wants a job done puts it into an elec­tronic sys­tem, and a per­son who wants work goes into the sys­tem and gets it. {124-C01}

He sorted it into three kinds. In cap­i­tal-intensive gigs the worker owns the asset: the Uber driver’s car, the Airbnb host’s house, the photographer’s ex­pen­sive equip­ment. In skill-intensive gigs, an Urban Company plumber or hair­dresser comes to your home. Microtasks are sent by firms to work­ers all over the world.
A de­liv­ery rider for Zepto, Swiggy or Zomato, he said, might get a flat fee plus some two ru­pees per kilo­me­tre, for the fuel and the two-wheeler he owns. {#perkm}
## More than a naka

This is more than an old street-corner naka gone dig­i­tal, Shah ar­gued. He went back to Ronald Coase’s paper *The Nature of the Firm*, which asks what a firm does in­side its bound­ary, with man­agers and tenured em­ploy­ees, and what it buys at arm’s length. {124-R01}

GPS, rat­ings and the dig­i­tal ex­haust work­ers leave be­hind now let an al­go­rithm do what a su­per­vi­sor of ten taxi driv­ers once did. The man­ager goes; the em­ployee be­comes an out­side con­trac­tor. The re­sult, Shah said, is higher pro­duc­tiv­ity and a big­ger GDP for a coun­try fight­ing mass poverty.
~ Hence his pro­posal of a Bharat Ratna for who­ever in­vented gig work, and Amit Varma’s ob­jec­tion that no cen­tral plan­ner did: it came out of spon­ta­neous order. {124-J02}

quote.text: Lo and be­hold, what have we done? A, we’ve sacked the man­ager be­cause now we no longer need the man­ager in­side the firm.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the boundary of the firm

sections.label: The charge sheet
sections.head: A fair hearing for the critics
sections.caption: the case against gig work
body: At Amit Varma’s re­quest, Ajay Shah first steel­manned the crit­ics, in three groups of com­plaints.

One is about work­ers: lost en­ti­tle­ments, volatile in­come, no ca­reer lad­der, no job se­cu­rity. Another is about al­go­rithms: a boss that watches more closely than any human, work­ers left atom­ised, rules that are opaque. The last is about AI: Indians paid low piece rates to train the sys­tems that will re­place them.
## Consenting adults

Shah began with free­dom and con­sent. Nobody forces a firm to post tasks or a worker to take them, any more than in a potato mar­ket, he said. He would ac­cept lim­its only for mi­nors, who can­not con­sent. {124-C03}
Training your re­place­ment is how in­dus­trial cap­i­tal­ism has al­ways worked, he ar­gued. In the Industrial Revolution, skilled work­ers were stud­ied to build bet­ter ma­chine tools. {124-C07}

An al­go­rith­mic boss is at least pre­dictable. And by George Akerlof’s logic in *The Market for ‘Lemons’*, close mon­i­tor­ing re­moves the in­for­ma­tion gap be­tween buyer and seller, which should push pay up, not down. {124-R02}
~ As for atom­i­sa­tion, “We are each in­di­vid­u­als,” Shah said. A worker who dis­likes Swiggy can try Zepto, then Urban Company.

quote.text: An al­go­rithm as a boss sounds bad. When you pause to think about it, it’s ac­tu­ally bril­liant.

portraits.caption: George Akerlof
portraits.credit: Yan Chi Vinci Chow, CC BY 3.0

sections.label: Ten reasons
sections.head: Hop on, hop off
sections.caption: ten reasons gig work is awesome
body: Amit Varma first un­der­lined Ajay Shah’s points with con­se­quences. People take gig work, he said, be­cause every other op­tion open to them is worse: un­em­ploy­ment, beg­ging or a job they like even less. {124-C04}
It is the case the hosts once made for sweat­shops[[x5]], pro­vided there is no co­er­cion or slav­ery.
Nor can plat­forms ex­ploit work­ers at will. There is no monop­sony, Varma said: Swiggy has to look after its peo­ple or they go to Zomato, and Zomato could lose them to Urban Company. {124-C06}
## Five, three and two
Then came his own ten rea­sons: five eco­nomic, three so­cial and two eth­i­cal. {124-C09}

The eco­nomic ones: gig work is a way into the city and into work; it lets work­ers hop be­tween plat­forms; it was there when COVID struck; rat­ings re­ward the con­sci­en­tious; and a vil­lage plumber can bor­row Urban Company’s net­work in­stead of need­ing a brand on day one.

The so­cial ones are in­clu­sion across caste and re­li­gion, choos­ing your own work-life bal­ance, and mov­ing cities or work­ing re­motely. The eth­i­cal ones are the dig­nity of work and the free­dom to de­cide whom you work for.

~ Today Swiggy, to­mor­row Zomato, Varma said, like the Cliff Richard song he placed in the 1960s: “Goodbye, Sam. Hello Samantha.” He did not think Cliff Richard was talk­ing about the gig econ­omy. {124-J08}

quote.text: They have cho­sen it be­cause it is the least de­mean­ing op­tion open to them.

sections.label: The Indian case
sections.head: Too few jobs, too much law
sections.caption: gig work in India
body: The over­whelm­ing prob­lem in India, Ajay Shah said, is that there is very lit­tle em­ploy­ment[[x8]]. About 440 mil­lion peo­ple work in a coun­try of 1.4 to 1.5 bil­lion.
Women’s labour force par­tic­i­pa­tion is about 10 per cent, he said, and about half of col­lege grad­u­ates are not work­ing. {#women}

So crit­ics who prize the pro­tec­tions of a for­mal job, which about 10 per cent of the pop­u­la­tion en­joys, are not being fair. “For 90% of India, what is great is hav­ing some in­come,” he said. {124-C10}
About one crore peo­ple do gig work, he es­ti­mated. “It’s a good num­ber. It’s a be­gin­ning. It is progress,” Shah said. {#crore}
## Room to work

Flexibility mat­ters most for women, who are bur­dened with house­work and child­care. “Do I want to do ten min­utes of work in a day? Do I want to do a hun­dred min­utes work in a day?” Shah asked, putting him­self in a woman’s place. {124-C12}

Indian labour law, he said, is deeply bro­ken. It treats a 10 per cent aris­toc­racy some­what well and leaves the rest out, so em­ploy­ers and work­ers alike turn to gig work. Amit Varma called the labour laws the fun­da­men­tal rea­son India missed its man­u­fac­tur­ing rev­o­lu­tion.
~ Gig work also eases mi­gra­tion: get the hang of Uber in Patna, Shah said, and the same app will carry you to Bhopal or Amdavad. {#patna}

quote.text: What Indian Labour Law does is it cre­ates vast un­em­ploy­ment in India. It pushes peo­ple out.

sections.label: The safety net
sections.head: Self-targeting, self-adjusting
sections.caption: gig work as the urban NREGS
body: India’s econ­o­mists long cham­pi­oned work­fare, Ajay Shah said: wel­fare with a catch, since you have to show up in the hot sun and break stones. The UPA gov­ern­ment made the idea na­tional as the NREGS.
Every now and then some­one pro­poses an NREGS for the cities[[x11]], with the gov­ern­ment of­fer­ing a hun­dred days of work. {#hundreddays} Shah fears a pop­ulist gov­ern­ment will one day do it.
He and Maitreesh Ghatak ar­gued in an ar­ti­cle that gig work is al­ready an urban safety net. {124-C13}
## The Parikh test
Professor Kirit Parikh, Shah re­called, used to say that NREGS was self-targeting, self-adjusting and self-liquidating. {124-S01}

Gig work, Shah ar­gued, passes the first two tests. Only peo­ple down on their luck take up de­liv­ery work, and sup­ply, de­mand and surge pric­ing set the price. It is not self-liquidating, and should not be: it is a per­ma­nent net under the urban econ­omy, the first port of call when COVID came.
Do-gooders, he said, should make sure ev­ery­one has the ba­sics: a smart­phone, UPI in and out, the abil­ity to read English on a screen, and two apps. {#upi}
~ Amit Varma’s gloss: “Public goods through vol­un­tary pri­vate ac­tion.”

quote.text: There should be this con­fi­dence and cer­tainty that if all else goes wrong, I al­ways have gig work.
Because for 90% of India, all that doesn’t exist. For 90% of India, what is great is hav­ing some in­come. All the things you talked about are a priv­i­lege.

p3.title: Stories from the street
p3.deck: A professor’s three selfs, an old naka, a slum and a caste-blind app

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on workfare, and Kirit Parikh’s favourite phrase
stories.head: The scheme that should have quit
body: In the West it is called work­fare, Ajay Shah said: wel­fare, but you have to show up in the hot sun and break some stones. Only peo­ple down on their luck se­lect them­selves for it. It has worked rea­son­ably well, he said.

A se­ries of pa­pers through the 1980s found sig­nif­i­cant ben­e­fits for the very poor­est from work­fare pro­grammes, for ex­am­ple in Maharashtra. {#eighties} The UPA gov­ern­ment then took the idea na­tional as the NREGS[[x10]]. Shah thinks the basic idea good, though he dis­agrees with its price points.
Professor Kirit Parikh had a phrase[[x9]] for it. “He used to say to me that the glory of NREGS is that it is self-targeting, self-adjusting, and self-liquidating,” Shah re­called. {124-S01}
Self-targeting, be­cause if you were well off, you wouldn’t go out and break stones. The sub­sidy reached the right peo­ple on its own.

Self-adjusting, be­cause when the har­vest did well, peo­ple pulled back, and when times were bad, they came. “You don’t need a gov­ern­ment, you don’t need an of­fi­cial to say we’ll have more NREGS, less NREGS,” Shah said.

And in the early 1990s Parikh told Shah the third part: when India be­came rich, no­body would want to work at 100 ru­pees a day. {#hundredrupees} Demand for the scheme would go away, and the pro­gramme would close it­self down.
~ “Sadly, that part didn’t work out,” Shah said. The wages NREGS paid were steadily bumped up through the years, dis­tort­ing the labour mar­ket, he said.
stories.why: The best wel­fare lets people’s own choices do the tar­get­ing and the scal­ing, with no of­fi­cial de­cid­ing who gets help. Once politi­cians fid­dle with the price, the pro­gramme loses the prop­erty that would have let it end. Shah ap­plied the same test to gig work. {124-C13}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Kirit Parikh’s three selfs

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the street-corner labour market
stories.head: Haggling at the chowk, now by app
body: For cen­turies, Ajay Shah said, Indian towns have had con­gre­ga­tion points, the naka or the chowk. Workers gather there, some­one who needs hands for a con­struc­tion project ar­rives, they hag­gle orally over a price, and peo­ple get a job for a day. {124-S02}

It is not a job with ten­ure, a monthly salary, a prov­i­dent fund, labour law or an HR de­part­ment to com­plain to. “It is just a very sim­ple pure spot mar­ket where there’s sup­ply and de­mand,” he said.
The taxi stand was the same: five or ten taxis wait­ing in one place for cus­tomers. “Perhaps if you’re in a bad city other than Bombay, you would ne­go­ti­ate a price,” Shah added. {124-J03}
~ Gig plat­forms, he said, are that old mar­ket with an elec­tronic layer on it.
stories.why: The sup­pos­edly new gig econ­omy is an old Indian ar­range­ment gone dig­i­tal. What is new is not the con­tract but the tech­nol­ogy un­der­neath, which changes where the bound­ary of the firm sits. {124-C02}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the naka and the taxi stand

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the city’s eyesore is really for
stories.head: The slum as a first address
body: When peo­ple in good urban apart­ments call slums an eye­sore and want them re­moved, Amit Varma is quick with two re­minders. {124-S04}
First, their do­mes­tic help and ev­ery­one they rely on live in slums. Second, in India at this mo­ment in time, slums are amaz­ing, be­cause they give peo­ple an entry point into the city[[x15]].

“If you’re from a vil­lage where are you going to live, you can’t re­ally af­ford to live any­where ex­cept in a slum,” he said. While the econ­omy is in this phase, a slum is a ticket to a bet­ter life.

~ Gig work, Varma ar­gued, works the same way: a vil­lager need not know some­one from his caste who knows some­body, but can sim­ply sign up on a plat­form. It was the first of his ten rea­sons why gig work is awe­some. {124-C09}
stories.why: Judge a rough-looking in­sti­tu­tion by the real next-best op­tion of the per­son using it, not by your own ideal. Remove the bot­tom rung of a lad­der and you lift no­body up; you lock them out.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on slums as an entry ticket

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the gig economy’s quiet inclusiveness
stories.head: Dinner doesn’t ask your caste
body: In Indian so­ci­ety, Amit Varma said, there are so many fault lines that it is very hard for a Dalit, for ex­am­ple, to get cer­tain kinds of job. A caste net­work, the wrong look or the wrong way of speak­ing can keep you out. {124-S05}
Gig plat­forms don’t ask. “Swiggy doesn’t give a shit what caste you are,” Varma said, and the build­ing wait­ing for its din­ner doesn’t ei­ther: it just wants the food on time.

He ad­mit­ted that some build­ings have a ter­ri­ble prac­tice of dis­crim­i­nat­ing against a Muslim de­liv­ery per­son. Delivery work­ers some­times smartly give an­other name at the door, he said, though they shouldn’t have to. {#nomdeplume}
~ But by and large, he ar­gued, caste and re­li­gion are no longer a bar­rier[[x3]] to get­ting a gig. It was per­haps the most im­por­tant of his rea­sons.
stories.why: The im­per­sonal plat­form, often crit­i­cised as de­hu­man­is­ing, qui­etly be­comes a force for in­clu­sion. In a so­ci­ety full of fault lines, an app that does not care who you are[[x4]] opens doors a caste net­work keeps shut.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 124. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Cliff Richard (Raph_PH, CC BY 2.0); Ronald Coase (University of Chicago Law School, Attribution); George Akerlof (Yan Chi Vinci Chow, CC BY 3.0).

shelf.title: The Nature of the Firm
shelf.creator: Ronald Coase
shelf.why: Coase’s an­swer to why firms exist when mar­kets can co­or­di­nate through prices: con­tract­ing is costly.

shelf.title: The Market for ‘Lemons’
shelf.creator: George Akerlof
shelf.why: Akerlof showed that when buy­ers can’t judge qual­ity, prices fall.

shelf.title: Why Gig Work Matters
shelf.creator: Maitreesh Ghatak and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ar­gues that gig work is a ready-made urban safety net that needs no gov­ern­ment, and an an­swer to re­cur­ring pop­ulist de­mands for an NREGS in the cities.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on KYC
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case that India’s KYC regime has mainly built mass sur­veil­lance of citizens’ fi­nances while never stop­ping a ter­ror­ist plot, and that the real dan­ger is a state watch­ing cit­i­zens and turn­ing its co­er­cive power on them.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on manufacturing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of why Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is weak: eight ways it dif­fers from ser­vices, twelve things that hob­ble it in India (from du­ties on im­ported in­puts to labour laws) and seven items for every state’s growth strat­egy.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on Luxury Beliefs
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on four papers
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

laughs.text: Amit’s made-up ori­gin story for the show. Sipping a bour­bon, he de­cided he needed a co-host and built a gig app called ‘Bourbon Company’ to find a new one every week. Week one, only Ajay ap­plied. Amit hoped pretty women or Bengali econ­o­mists might apply next, but weeks two and three it was Ajay again. ‘So the gig econ­omy is a strange and cu­ri­ous thing. What should have been a one-night stand be­came an af­fair.’ He then asks Ajay to re­spond to his ‘mag­nif­i­cent so­lil­o­quy.’

Amit on set­ting your own work-life bal­ance: ‘If I am a Bengali who wants an af­ter­noon nap, I will nap in the af­ter­noon. Mera Uber app bandh hai, and then I will go out and drive in the evening.’

Ajay sug­gests that do-gooders ‘round up every urban teenager, boys and girls, and take them into camps and teach them the ba­sics of how to get gig work.’ Amit steps in: ‘No, you didn’t lit­er­ally mean this. No one should go and take young peo­ple... Because young peo­ple, out of their own in­cen­tives, will fig­ure it out.’

Amit de­scribes a gig worker hop­ping plat­forms (‘Today is Swiggy, tomorrow’s Zomato’) with a Cliff Richard song he places in the 1960s: ‘Goodbye Sam, Hello Samantha... Goodbye Lou, Hello Louise.’ He adds: ‘I don’t think Cliff Richard was talk­ing about the gig econ­omy.’
